assignments.reason: The act of explaining Torah in the vernacular is essentially the tzaddik's Mashiach-dimension self-sacrifice for Israel. Its essential nature is not a neutral linguistic act but an expression of the tzaddik-of-the-generation's role: just as Mashiach bears suffering for Israel (סָבֵל מַרְעִין), the tzaddik lowers the Torah into accessible language as an act of holy self-lowering. The Torah frames this explicitly as a consequence of being bechina of Mashiach (line 6: 'וְהַיְנוּ מַה שֶּׁאָמַרְנוּ'). Its essential nature belongs to the domain of the tzaddik-Moshe-Mashiach archetype — it is what the tzaddik *does* in virtue of being Mashiach.

Despite the word 'chol' (profane), this concept's essential nature in Torah #118 is not generic profanity but specifically the state of being 'מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵינוּ' — the Mashiach's wound-bearing, his becoming-profane-for-Israel's-sake. The Zohar citation (דְּאִתְעֲבִד חֹל בְּגִינַיְהוּ) defines this as a dimension of the Mashiach's suffering, not a standalone concept of secularity. Its essential nature is the sacrificial lowering that defines the Mashiach-tzaddik role — it is what happens to the tzaddik's Torah *because he is Mashiach*. Polarity is good because this is a holy self-sacrifice (לְכַפֵּר עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל), not an evil state.
